items.title: The English Channel is not getting narrower
items.claim: Is the English Channel closing as Britain and France converge?

options.text: Yes, by about 1 cm per year
No — there is no convergent plate boundary; both sit on the Eurasian plate. The Channel was carved by megaflood erosion around 450,000 and 160,000 years ago
Yes, by about 1 metre per year
It widens by 10 cm per year

items.reveal:
Britain was connected to mainland Europe as recently as 8,000 years ago (the Doggerland landscape). The Channel itself was formed by catastrophic megafloods when a glacial lake in the southern North Sea breached a chalk ridge at Dover-Calais (Gupta et al., Nature 2007).

Both Britain and France sit on the Eurasian plate, with no relative motion at this scale. The 'closing' or 'opening' claim is geophysically wrong.

Isostatic rebound is causing northern Britain to rise and southern England to sink — relative sea level rises faster on the south coast.
items.why: Plausible-sounding numerical claims about geographic change can be entirely fictional. The right test is mechanism, not vivid number — there's no plate boundary to drive Channel closure.

items.title: The Gulf Stream warms western Europe by an estimated 5 °C
items.claim: How much does ocean circulation warm western Europe?

options.text: Not at all — climate is determined by latitude alone

Comparison with similar-latitude locations (Calgary, Labrador) and modelling studies suggest the wider North Atlantic circulation system contributes around 5-10 °C of additional warmth to western Europe
By 30 °C — without it Europe would be like Antarctica

items.reveal:
The Gulf Stream is the western boundary current of the North Atlantic gyre; it broadens north of Cape Hatteras into the North Atlantic Current. Prevailing westerlies carry the heat onshore.

Richard Seager and colleagues (2002) argued that atmospheric heat transport and the southwesterly stationary wave (set up by the Rocky Mountains) are at least as important as ocean heat in distinguishing western from eastern continental winters. The single-cause 'Gulf Stream warms Britain' story is too simple.

The AMOC (Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation) has weakened by an estimated 15% since the mid-20th century (Caesar et al., 2018, 2021). A collapse would cool Europe and warm the tropics.
items.why: Climate is the product of multiple systems acting together. The Gulf Stream story is partly true and partly simplified; a teaching answer needs both the ocean and the atmosphere.

items.title: Spearman's rank correlation goes from -1 to +1
items.claim: What does Spearman's rank correlation coefficient measure?

options.text: The strength and direction of monotonic association between ranked variables, between -1 (perfect negative) and +1 (perfect positive); 0 indicates no monotonic relationship
The mean of the two variables

items.reveal:
Spearman's ρ uses ranks rather than raw values, making it robust to outliers and non-linear monotonic relationships. Pearson's r requires a linear relationship and normally-distributed data.

Critical values must be checked against sample size: with n=10, ρ must exceed about 0.564 to be significant at p=0.05. With n=30, the threshold is about 0.306.

A strong correlation can be coincidental, confounded by a third variable, or reversed in direction (Simpson's paradox). 'Correlation does not imply causation' is a methodological starting point, not a slogan.
items.why: Statistical reasoning is part of geographical skills. Strong correlation is evidence, not proof — geographers must argue causation separately from association, ideally through mechanism.
